title: Real Property Interests & Conveyancing
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: Which is NOT required for a deed to be valid between the original parties?
rationales: Writing is required under the Statute of Frauds.
A competent grantor is required.
Correct. Recording is not required for validity between the parties; it affects priority and notice.
Delivery and acceptance are required.

options: Not required for a valid deed; a gift deed can be valid
rationales: Consideration is not a deed-validity requirement.
Correct. A deed can be valid without consideration, as in a gift deed.
This is not specific to quitclaims.
This is not specific to trust deeds.

options: Physical handover of the paper only
The grantor's present intent to immediately convey, plus acceptance
rationales: Physical handover alone is neither necessary nor sufficient.
Correct. Present intent to convey immediately, plus acceptance, is the legal test.
Recording is unrelated to delivery.
Grantees are not required to sign deeds.

questions.stem: A grantor signs a deed 'to my daughter' and keeps it in a locked box with intent that it take effect only at death. This deed is most likely:
options: Invalid for lack of present intent to convey and delivery during life
Valid because it is in writing and signed
rationales: There was no present intent to convey during the grantor's lifetime.
Correct. Without present intent and delivery during life, this functions as an invalid attempted testamentary transfer.
Recording after death does not cure the defect.
Writing and signature alone are not sufficient without delivery and present intent.

questions.stem: A grant deed's implied warranties generally do NOT cover:
options: Prior conveyance by the grantor to someone else
Defects arising before the grantor's ownership
Undisclosed liens created by the grantor
rationales: This is covered by implied warranty.
This is covered by implied warranty.
Correct. Grant deed warranties do not reach back before the grantor's own ownership.
This is covered by implied warranty.

options: Warrants clear title against all claims
Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties
Cannot be used between family members
Automatically transfers ownership even if the grantor has no interest
rationales: That describes a warranty deed, not a quitclaim.
Correct. A quitclaim conveys only whatever interest exists, with no warranties at all.
Quitclaims are commonly used between family members and ex-spouses.
A quitclaim cannot convey an interest the grantor does not have.

questions.stem: An ex-spouse signs a document conveying whatever community-property interest he may have in the family home to his former wife as part of a divorce settlement. The appropriate instrument is most likely a:
rationales: Warranty deeds are rare in California and unnecessary here.
A trust deed is a security instrument, not applicable here.
Correct. A quitclaim is the customary tool for clearing a specific person's potential claim on title.
A reconveyance deed releases a trust deed lien, which is not the situation here.

questions.stem: A trust deed (deed of trust) functions primarily as:
options: A security instrument conveying bare legal title to a trustee
rationales: It is not a conveyance of full beneficial ownership.
Correct. It secures a debt by conveying bare legal title to a trustee, reconveyed upon payoff.
It is unrelated to interspousal quitclaims.
It is unrelated to eminent domain.

options: Is required for the deed to be valid between the parties
Eliminates the need for title insurance
rationales: Title transfers upon valid execution and delivery, not recording.
Correct. Recording gives constructive notice and helps establish priority among competing claims.
Recording is not required for validity between the original parties.
Recording does not eliminate the value of title insurance.

questions.stem: A distressed seller sells the same property to Buyer A and Buyer B. Buyer A's deed is delivered first but not recorded for two weeks. Buyer B, unaware of Buyer A's purchase, pays value and records immediately. Under California recording principles, priority most likely favors:
options: Buyer A, because delivery occurred first
Buyer B, because Buyer B paid value and recorded first without notice
The seller, who may resell to a third buyer
rationales: Earlier delivery alone does not guarantee priority against a later good-faith recorder.
Correct. A subsequent purchaser for value who records first without notice of the prior unrecorded interest can gain priority.
Possession is not the controlling factor in this scenario.
The seller has no continuing right to resell after conveying to Buyer A.

options: The law treats a recorded document as known regardless of actual knowledge
A notice was posted on the property only
rationales: That describes actual notice.
Correct. Constructive notice is imputed by recording, whether or not someone actually looked.
Verbal warnings are not constructive notice.
Physical posting alone is not the legal mechanism described.

questions.stem: A legal description referencing directions, distances, and monuments from a fixed point of beginning is called:
rationales: Government survey uses township, range, and section.
Correct. Metes and bounds describes property by directions, distances, and monuments.
Lot, block, and tract references a recorded subdivision map.
An APN is an assessment identifier, not a full legal description.

questions.stem: A street address alone is generally:
options: A sufficient legal description for a deed
Not treated as a sufficient legal description for a deed
Required in addition to metes and bounds
rationales: A street address alone is not treated as sufficient.
Correct. Deeds require a legal description sufficient to identify the property with reasonable certainty.
It is not a formal requirement alongside metes and bounds.
This is not limited to commercial property.

questions.stem: An ambiguous legal description that conflicts with the assessor's parcel number is best understood as:
options: A title problem that may require a surveyor or quiet title action to resolve
Something only the buyer's lender needs to worry about
rationales: It is not irrelevant; it can cloud title.
Correct. Ambiguous descriptions are title problems requiring resolution before a clean closing.
Escrow does not automatically cure description defects.
It affects buyer, seller, and lender alike.

questions.stem: Acquiring title through open, notorious, hostile, and continuous possession under claim of right, combined with tax payment for the statutory period, describes:
rationales: Eminent domain is a government taking with compensation.
Correct. This describes adverse possession.
Devise is transfer under a valid will.
Intestate succession applies when there is no valid will.

questions.stem: When a person dies without a valid will, real property passes by:
rationales: Devise requires a valid will.
Correct. Intestate succession governs distribution when there is no valid will.
Adverse possession requires possession over time, unrelated to death.
Eminent domain is a government taking.

questions.stem: Escrow delivery of a deed, where a grantor deposits a signed deed with instructions to deliver upon satisfying conditions, is generally treated as:
options: Invalid until the grantor personally hands over the deed
Valid delivery once conditions are met, sometimes relating back to the deposit date
The same as a testamentary transfer
rationales: Escrow delivery is a recognized valid delivery method.
Correct. This is valid delivery once conditions are satisfied, and can relate back under the relation-back doctrine.
It is common in both residential and commercial transactions.
It is distinct from a testamentary transfer, which requires will formalities.

questions.stem: A licensee cannot advise a client on which vesting to choose because:
options: Vesting never matters to the client
That is a legal/tax determination outside license scope
Vesting is fixed by the assessor
rationales: Vesting has real legal and financial consequences for the client.
Correct. Vesting choice implicates legal and tax consequences beyond license scope; refer to an attorney or CPA.
Lenders do not choose vesting for the buyer.
The assessor does not determine vesting.
